title: The Post-18 Project: Civic at the crossroads
summary: Richard Brabner argues that if civic is to become a core expectation of universities, it must be treated as a core priority
full_text:
The top line

Universities’ civic role has had plenty of warm words from government and very little structural support. Every lever that shapes how universities behave – regulation, the REF, funding – was built for a different job, by people who answer for something other than place. No one owns the relationship between a university and its place, so civic work depends on goodwill, and it is the first thing to go when money is tight.

What should be done

Give the relationship an owner: a new statutory duty for the Office for Students to have regard to place, mandatory Civic University Agreements co-signed by local and regional government, and catalyst support for regional university networks. In the meantime, fix the incentives: tie the Strategic Priorities Grant and a larger, civic-linked HEIF to those agreements. For the longer term, make place a term of reference for any tertiary review, and bring higher education, skills and research into a single department.

The bottom line

Universities cannot be asked to do more for place while operating within a system that too often rewards the opposite. If civic is to become a core expectation, it must be treated as a core priority.

Civic 2.0

Civic 2.0 is a programme to engage national and regional policymakers in the economic and social role higher education institutions play in their towns, cities and regions. The programme aims to help politicians and policymakers come up with policies and incentives which enable this positive role to expand, helping the social and economic development of towns and cities up and down the country.

The partners of the programme include the Invest in UK University R&D Campaign hosted by Midlands Innovation, some of the founding university partners from the Civic University Network, including Birmingham, Newcastle and Queen Mary, and the National Co-ordinating Centre for Public Engagement (NCCPE).

Methodology

The Policy Signal is based on research conducted by the author for Civic 2.0. Twenty recorded semi-structured interviews and two semi-structured meetings were held between January and March 2026 with higher education leaders and policymakers. Ten were with current or former vice-chancellors and pro-vice-chancellors; the others were with executives of sector bodies and thought leaders on the place/civic agenda. The themes that emerged from the interviews form the basis of this Policy Signal, and all quotes are unattributed under the Chatham House Rule. The Policy Signal also draws on the author’s experience of leading and shaping the civic university movement over the past eight years.

In the opening months of Keir Starmer’s Government there was renewed hope for the civic university movement. Not only did Bridget Phillipson’s letter to Vice-Chancellors in the autumn of 2024 include the civic role as one of the Government’s five priorities for higher education, but the Government’s other key priorities – supporting economic growth and the access and opportunity agenda – had clear ‘place’ dimensions to them too.5 It seemed as though the civic agenda might be given a new lease of life after the Covid years and the previous Government’s failure to deliver on levelling-up. Yet, as one university leader said in a rather understated fashion: “I’m a bit disappointed in government…I thought there was that sense in Bridget’s letter that civic was one of the five things. I struggled to see how that’s come drawn through to the white paper. Can’t really see it there.” The same interviewee then offered a sage piece of advice: “As ever, look at what they do, not what they say.”

This critique was prevalent amongst many of the university leaders, academics and policy makers interviewed as part of the Civic 2.0 initiative. These interviews were run primarily to help shape a strategy for Civic 2.0 – a programme to engage national and regional policymakers in the economic and social role higher education institutions play in their towns, cities and regions. The interviews also provide fascinating insights into the future of the civic agenda: what is working, what needs to improve, the barriers to civic engagement, the opportunities, and the policy ideas that could strengthen it.

There was a strong perception from the interviewees that civic is at a crossroads. The optimistic view, according to participants, is that the Civic University Commission and successor initiatives such as the National Civic Impact Accelerator (NCIA) have helped to revitalise the agenda. These national programmes “moved the dial” on how universities think about place. The main recommendation from the Commission – the establishment of Civic University Agreements, co-produced with local actors such as local authorities – was adopted by large swathes of the sector and has led to meaningful cultural change, as universities no longer see engagement with their city or region as a peripheral activity, but as core. Most significant of all was the perception that a moral consensus has taken root. Several participants said that they do ‘civic’ because it is the right thing to do, even if the financial climate makes delivery harder.

Having said that, most interviewees described a sector in survival mode, where inflation, the falling unit of resource, and the aftershocks of the pandemic and geopolitics have forced institutions to prioritise solvency over their place role. The university leader’s critique of government – that rhetoric about place has not been matched by coherent policy or funding mechanisms – was common. Universities operate within regulatory systems that reward competition over collaboration, and civic work therefore remains largely voluntary – a “nice to have” when budgets allow, rather than a core expectation.

The interviews therefore highlighted a paradox at the heart of the civic agenda: it is a moral mission which is central to the future of higher education, while also in danger of losing momentum because of the lack of incentives in the system. It is this paradox that has paralysed the place/civic agenda for some time. Successive governments have spoken positively about the role of universities in their places but have treated delivery as the universities’ job, because a moral mission shouldn’t require an incentive. Much of the university sector, meanwhile, recognises the importance of its civic role, but the fear of losing out in a market system which rewards institutions that follow the incentives is paramount, particularly when universities are in survival mode.

Compounding the moral/incentive paradox, the system has been designed with no independent agency responsible for the relationship between the university and its place. This has meant that the quality of partnerships is overly dependent on local leadership and relationships, rather than a structure or system which is embedded. As a result, partnerships and practice can be inconsistent across (and within) different regions. The ad hoc nature of devolution in the country also contributes to a broader system where regional partnerships are structurally more important in some places than others. Giving the relationship an owner is therefore the starting point for the recommendations in this paper.

On paper, at least, Andy Burnham’s government offers something different. Someone who has not only spoken positively about the civic agenda but ‘lived’ it as Mayor of Greater Manchester. An advocate for devolution and local placemaking, when he gave oral evidence to the Civic University Commission several years ago, he called for a partnership between devolved government and universities to offer ‘golden handcuffs’ to students going into public sector careers as a way to enable graduate retention in regions outside of London.6 Not then someone who relies on the ‘invisible hand’ or what we might regard today as the automatic benefit of universities in their places stimulating local economic growth through their presence and spending power, but someone who sees the value of intervention to enhance that role further. Someone who believes in an ‘intentional’ civic role. Someone who may be interested in creating the frameworks for a system which works for every region.

It is with this in mind that this Policy Signal for The Post-18 Project asks who should own the relationship between universities and their places, and what incentives should flow from that design change to enable universities and government to work in effective partnership, so that civic can, as the Secretary of State’s letter in 2024 put it, ‘form a core part of a renewed vision for the sector.’7

Before we get to the barriers holding the civic university movement back, it is worth noting that the civic university agenda has long suffered from definitional ambiguity. For many it is synonymous with local community and place, though its geographic boundaries are often porous. For others, place is too restrictive – they build on the view of civic as citizenship, and have a ‘social value’ view of civic, which is less about geography than about the university’s contribution to society. Civic is also seen by some as linked to cities, particularly if we hark back to the original ‘civic universities’ in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Does that mean that universities in towns or rural settings can’t be ‘civic’? And then there is the question about what civic universities do; with parts of the civic movement emphasising public and community engagement, and others focusing on economic impact.

The broad and varied definition of a civic university is a challenge. If it can mean almost anything, it can mean almost nothing. The lack of clarity often encourages a PR-led approach to being civic, where almost anything can be described as civic, and weakens the case to government and policy makers to incentivise this role. This challenge was also picked up by some of the interviewees who were critical of the framing of civic, which they claim can be confusing to external stakeholders not versed in the language of higher education.

It is therefore important to be upfront about the definition this paper uses when it discusses the civic role, and subsequently the type of incentives required to stimulate the civic role. First, this paper uses a geographically rooted concept of civic. It is about a university’s local place and not a broader social value definition. The majority of participants viewed civic and place in almost synonymous terms and this paper agrees with them. While the geographic boundaries are porous and depend on the specific issue, the civic partnership and the nature of local or regional government in any particular area, the civic role can essentially be hyper-local (town-gown), town or city-wide, or regional. What it is not, for example, is a university in London running a widening participation initiative in the North West of England, nor a university in the UK running projects in other countries. They may have immense value, but they are not what this paper considers to be civic.

Intentional vs incidental

The other definitional theme common throughout the interviews was the concept of intentionality. Every university has an economic, social, environmental and cultural impact on its place, whether or not it regards ‘civic’ as a core principle or mission for the institution. Often universities look to measure and publicise this impact. This type of impact – the spending power of its students and staff, the amount spent by the institution on its supply chain and so on – is the incidental impact of a university on its place. Incidental or ‘automatic’, because it is not based on the needs of the place but simply a result of the institution having a physical presence. The irony of our unplanned system is that universities’ impact on their place can be, and is often, unrelated to civic intent. It is the case that several universities that have less mature civic missions have a big impact on their place because they have grown student numbers, and others that are strategically embedded in their places have less of an automatic impact because they have been the institutional losers in a market-based system. This has been felt particularly acutely since the removal of the cap on UK undergraduate numbers. One by-product of this system is that local economies and societies are affected by a system where no entity – national, regional or local – can steer it in a way that supports any particular place or the priorities of the day.

This lack of levers is core to the barriers set out below, but it also means that the civic role based on strategic intent is even more important. The participants consistently spoke about civic engagement needing to be woven through institutional strategy and decision-making, not a patchwork of well-meant initiatives. “A civic university is about having a clearly articulated civic intent strategy, which is where you go beyond the kind of incidental civic aspects… and you go, this is our priority. So it’s about making choices about how your institution best delivers for the place and the institutions and the communities that it’s there.” This view was at the heart of the original Civic University Commission’s recommendation to establish Civic University Agreements in partnership with other civic actors such as local authorities. The purpose of these agreements was to analyse the needs of a place, including engagement with stakeholders and all parts of the local community, and then shape a strategy and plan off the back of this analysis. Putting the needs of the place first rather than what the institution had always done.

While the quality of delivery inevitably varies – more than 70 universities have publicly committed to having such agreements, and 59 CUAs are already extant8 – it was clear from the interviews that participants agreed with a definition of the civic role focused on the university being intentionally rather than incidentally civic. In short, the civic role is the intentional contribution a university makes to the economic, social, cultural, and environmental wellbeing of its town, city, or region. As a result, this paper looks at the barriers and levers to unlock the intentional civic role, rather than simply the general local impact of the institution.

With this paper’s definition of the civic university clear, what then, as expressed by the interviewees, is holding the civic university back at a time when the external environment has got harder?

According to the participants, there are three main barriers to universities playing a more substantive role in their places.

Lack of resources and bandwidth for the civic role

Regulatory architecture and incentives which prioritise other things and ultimately undermine the civic role

Civic as a victim of the machinery of government

Resources and bandwidth

Given the financial state of the sector, it almost goes without saying that resourcing civic activity is a key challenge. However, it is worth noting a few particular aspects of how the financial crisis in universities impacts the civic agenda beyond the higher education equivalent of Liam Byrne’s ‘there’s no money left’ letter.

First, participants reported a disconnect between what universities are expected to deliver in civic terms and the financial incentives available. Given the sector’s finances it is very difficult to prioritise anything which doesn’t offer a financial return in the short-term, and without dedicated funding, civic activity competes poorly against activities with a clearer financial return. From a pure financial perspective, universities face an ‘opportunity cost’ when they prioritise and deliver civic activity.

Second, a key word used time and time again by the interviewees was ‘bandwidth’. With the majority of the university sector going through some form of restructuring as a result of the financial crisis, there is a lack of time and capacity for colleagues – academic and professional – to prioritise civic and place. As one sector expert said: “People are doing more work with less resources. It just means that keeping something going becomes harder”. Many of the respondents also focussed on the bandwidth of partners across the public and private sectors who are themselves going through similar financial challenges, and the difficulty they have with the capacity to partner effectively with universities. One described an MOU where only a single person remained from either the university or partner organisation three years later, with the loss of institutional memory that implies.

Third, as concerns about bandwidth imply, civic engagement requires sustained relationship-building, yet a further complication is that, even when projects are funded with a place-dimension, project-based funding programmes operate on compressed timescales. One participant noted that funding cycles of three years, with 18 months lost to recruitment and setup, leave insufficient time for genuine partnership development. The lack of structural funding incentivises a transactional approach to civic engagement rather than one which is embedded.

Regulatory architecture and incentives

As important as funding are the regulatory incentives in the system. Despite warm words, successive governments have provided no coherent framework signalling that civic engagement matters. Multiple respondents noted that without either regulatory requirement or dedicated ‘carrot and stick’ incentives, civic activity becomes “charisma-driven and entirely optional” – vulnerable to being cut when financial pressure mounts.

The interviewees picked out several inter-linking factors which contribute to this. First, there is no universal definition or expectation of what civic engagement means, and no system for assessing whether institutions are meeting civic obligations. Participants suggested a framework distinguishing between “must do,” “should do,” and “may do” activities, with corresponding enforcement mechanisms. Currently, civic engagement sits entirely in the voluntary “may do” category.

Second, and more specifically, respondents noted that the Office for Students was designed as a market regulator focused on competition, not collaboration or civic outcomes. The Higher Education and Research Act 2017 emphasises competition, providing no incentive for inter-institutional collaboration or partnership with FE colleges. Several participants noted that while there are signs of the OfS beginning to consider place and growth, the fundamental design works against civic objectives.

Third, the Research Excellence Framework emerged as a major barrier, with its disciplinary focus actively discouraging the interdisciplinary, place-based research that civic engagement requires. Academics operate on long-term REF cycles, and anything not contributing to four-star papers or impact case studies struggles for attention. One participant noted that academics “have a different currency to the outside world” – if civic work cannot be translated into REF impact, engagement drops dramatically. The participants also acknowledged that other academic reward systems such as the Teaching Excellence Framework and to a lesser extent the Knowledge Exchange Framework were also discouraging civic engagement. The overall system effect is that career progression rewards global publications over local impact; and rankings systems drive behaviours that maximise international citations rather than regional benefit.

Fourth, participants regularly highlighted a disconnect between skills policy and university incentives. Until the Lifelong Learning Entitlement (LLE) is properly implemented, there is little financial incentive for universities to serve local adult populations outside traditional degree programmes. Skills England, local skills improvement plans, and mayoral ambitions for skills devolution create a complex landscape where nobody is clearly incentivised or empowered to coordinate universities with local workforce needs.

None of the levers described above was built with place in mind, and each is working as designed. The REF is doing its job; so are the OfS, Skills England and the other ways universities are measured (the KEF, the TEF and so on). In their own right, each causes significant problems for the civic and place role. That is bad enough, but combine a regulator which prioritises competition to the exclusion of place, a reward system like the REF which discourages interdisciplinary place-based research, and the lack of any entity coordinating universities with local workforce needs, and the result is an atomised system with few, if any, levers to enact change quickly. That no one is responsible for how the system collectively affects place is a significant problem not only for higher education in England, but a missed opportunity for places up and down the country where universities could play a bigger and more positive role.

Machinery of government

The civic university agenda also falls victim to failures within the machinery of government. Respondents were highly critical of the Department for Education, saying that it had no or little concept of place. But they also recognised that higher education sits across multiple departments: DfE for teaching, DSIT (when the interviews took place, now DBIST) for research. This fragmentation makes coherent place-based policy difficult for ministers and civil servants alike as there is no government department looking at the system as a whole.

Participants raised several other concerns about the machinery of government that hold back the civic agenda. In the non-HE and research government departments, respondents often said there was a lack of cut through and understanding of how the civic/place role of universities could help them deliver their priorities. The Pride in Place strategy was cited as the classic example: it does not mention universities once, which compares unfavourably to a range of sectors including health, sport, culture, policing, FE and schools. Beyond Pride in Place, multiple respondents cited MHCLG as difficult to engage with on questions of universities’ role in place.

Outside of Whitehall, respondents often lamented the demise of Regional Development Agencies (despite this occurring well over a decade ago). One interviewee described it as “one of the most stupid pieces of policy making”. The RDAs provided funding, coordination, and incentives for universities to engage regionally. Their replacements have not matched the RDAs’ scale, responsibility, and resources. Linked to this there were mixed views amongst the participants about devolution. While it was seen as by far the biggest opportunity for the civic agenda, particularly for universities in areas that have or are developing mayoral combined authorities with growing capacity, participants from universities outside of these areas (‘devo deserts’) were concerned about a two-tier approach to policy making, where they would lose out because of a slower pace to devolution in their region.

Given the environment universities are working in and the barriers identified by the interviewees, the civic and place role of universities is increasingly reliant on a community of senior university leaders and practitioners who see it as the right thing to do – progressive colleagues in the sector who prioritise the civic despite incentives pointing in other directions. But however strong the argument that this is correct – that it is a moral imperative and universities should just get on with it – the effect is to penalise the universities which focus on civic and place, because any activity done despite the incentives carries a clear opportunity cost for the university. With the sector facing severe financial constraints, those who are able to prioritise the civic will over time become fewer and fewer. With the Government saying that civic and place is one of its five priorities, this is a key example of the system working against the stated aims of the government. If civic really is a priority, this does not seem to be a sensible or sustainable way forward.

Instead, we need to shift the system towards what Lord Kerslake would always refer to as ‘enlightened self-interest’: a true long-term partnership between universities and their places, enabled by a system which recognises the holistic role of universities in their towns, cities and regions, and which benefits local communities and universities alike. But self-interest can only be enlightened if someone owns the system that defines it – which is why ownership comes first in what follows.

By the very nature of universities and their places, the full answer to shifting the system in a more civic direction cuts across Whitehall, spans local, regional, national and international policymaking, and touches several government priorities. Indeed, the collection of recommendations below align particularly well with the Government’s Rewiring the State agenda, which aims to strengthen local and regional institutions, devolve decision making and provide stronger local accountability.9

There is much to be said for how government could enable universities in partnership with other sectors to play a bigger role in supporting local economic growth, healthy communities and improving people’s quality of life in a range of different ways, and the intention of the Civic 2.0 campaign is to unlock some of these ideas. But, as the interviews clearly express, there are barriers and blockages within the higher education and research policy landscape – the ‘bread and butter’ of university policy – which are the focus of this Policy Signal.

We also need to factor in that higher education is not at the top of the government’s agenda at the moment, and with significant economic and geopolitical challenges deepening, that is unlikely to change in the near future. We continue to be in a period of scarcity and any pragmatic approach to enhancing the civic role has to reflect reality, rather than promote wishful thinking.

Having said that, whether the sector should advocate for fiscally neutral policies to support civic and place was a bone of contention amongst the interviewees. For example, one said “I don’t think one should encourage people to think that things are free”,whereas others thought it was the right, pragmatic approach. Some of the respondents also emphasised that additional regulatory or data requirements would put financial burdens on HEIs and would be unwelcome, whereas others thought it was the best way to change institutions. Many interviewees also noted that universities are very adept at responding to small pots of funding or even ministerial direction, whereas others said the whole system needed to change, or that only a small number of system-wide incentives would make a real difference.

With that in mind, the way ahead needs to look at both incremental changes and systemic reforms. This is not a deliberate fudge. Given the current fiscal environment, it is wise to consider incremental incentives which government could adopt to support the civic role in the short term. That may mean some additional resource for the civic role – ideally a small amount of new money, but if necessary created through efficiencies elsewhere in the system – reflecting the fact that there is little financial headroom.

But we should not lose sight of the fact that meaningful change requires strategic system-wide reform. With the rapidly changing political weather (in particular the change to a multi-party system, with populist parties on the left and right), and the growing importance of the ‘graduate voter’ who is typically not best pleased with the repayment system, there is a possibility that higher education could rapidly move up the political agenda in the future. If this creates the space for the higher or tertiary system to be reshaped, civic must be at the heart of this change.

The following recommendations are focussed on supporting universities’ place role in the short and longer-term. They are limited to the higher education and research policy arenas and are directed at tackling who has responsibility for the civic role, system changes required to elevate the positive impact on place, and the three main barriers and blockages to universities being civic (the way they are funded, regulated and measured).

The recommendations are grouped by what they do:

Ownership of civic – who is responsible for the relationship between a university and its place

Interim incentives – fixes to funding and measurement while ownership beds in

System change – place as one of the terms of any future settlement

In isolation the recommendations provide incremental change and help – in a limited way – to incentivise the civic role. Collectively, they offer a strategic and systemic approach to helping universities have a bigger positive economic and social impact on the places they are part of.

Further reports will be published looking at how universities’ place role can be enhanced through policy outside of HE and Research.

A. Ownership of civic

These recommendations focus on the gap in responsibility for the civic place agenda, and detail ways to enable regulatory and institutional ownership of the agenda. Taken together, they amount to a constitution-in-embryo for place: an owner, a binding agreement, a counterparty with a seat at the table, and a collective regional voice.

1. OfS to become responsible body for civic/place

The OfS would become the responsible body for civic/place, and would give the university-place relationship an owner for the first time.

To do this, the government should introduce legislation so that the OfS is given a new statutory duty to have regard to place. This would formally promote collaboration between higher education providers and Further Education to ensure the right skills provision within each region, promote collaboration with other key public and private sectors in the university’s region, promote student choice and opportunity in each region, promote the efficient use of resources and value for money through collaborative working and services. As part of this, the OfS would become the responsible body ensuring each university has an effective partnership with its place. This must not become prescriptive, as each place is different, but would ensure each university adheres to an appropriate process in formalising effective relationships with stakeholders in their region.

2. Mandatory Civic University Agreements

Many universities have co-produced Civic University Agreements over the last seven years. These Agreements – locally developed – have made a tangible difference by putting the strategic needs of the place at the heart of a university’s approach. These agreements also recognise that each place has its own challenges and opportunities and any national programme which prescribed what should be in each Agreement would fail. However, as this is an entirely voluntary approach by universities there is little incentive to measure progress, and the quality and delivery of the Agreements are patchy across the country. In that regard, the Office for Students and UKRI should make this a mandatory exercise and require universities to submit a civic strategy and plan (this could be a reformed Civic University Agreement) for their civic area (this could be as a single university, or an Agreement which covers multiple universities in a place). The reformed agreements would include a plan for the skills and innovation provision for their region, alongside other priorities co-produced and co-signed with local and regional government. Each reformed Agreement would include long-term goals and annual milestones. There would be an expectation that the signatories of the Agreement would report annually on progress. For universities that wish to have access to government funding for civic activity (see recommendations on incentives), a Civic Agreement / Strategy would be required.

3. Local and/or regional government on the board of Civic University Agreements

Alongside local and/or regional government shaping Civic University Agreements, there would be a requirement for them to be represented on any Civic Agreement Board which would not only produce the civic plan for the region, but also report annually on progress. This would ensure local and/or regional government has a stake in the civic priorities and how any funding for place is spent.

4. Catalyst support for regional networks

With increasing devolution and the need for universities to work together in their regions to speak as a collective voice to mayors, business and national government; the Office for Students and Research England should work with the sector to help to catalyse and foster regional networks of universities, like Midlands Innovation, London Higher, Yorkshire Universities, the newly formed West of England Universities and Universities North East. While universities should fund these networks, there could be a small amount of catalyst support (up to £5m) to develop new regional networks where required, to support the skills provision within these networks, and to form a national voice so that these emerging networks can themselves speak as one to national government. There should also be an expectation from the OfS and Research England that when collaborative bidding opportunities arise, they are directed via the regional networks.

B. Interim incentives

While the policy will to support the civic agenda should follow once the agenda has an owner, there is an urgent need in the meantime to fix the incentives that shape universities’ civic role.

5. Strategic Priorities Grant and Strategic Priorities Funding

Access to certain funding opportunities would be open to universities that have a Civic Agreement. This would include a larger Strategic Priorities Grant from the OfS and any future Strategic Priorities Funding from UKRI, ensuring that universities, government and agencies incentivise and prioritise the impact a university has on its place.

6. HEIF and KEF

There is currently a significant debate about who has control of HEIF funding, whether it should be controlled centrally or devolved. As per recommendation 3, the reformed Civic Agreements could provide a way for regional government to shape the priorities for how the funding is spent, even if the funding pot remains within Research England.

Beyond the current debate, the Government could look to review its longer-term approach to HEIF. In particular, the Office for Students and Research England could be directed to evaluate whether HEIF should be linked formally with the Knowledge Exchange Framework. The purpose would be to provide credibility to the KEF and simultaneously have an additional mechanism to measure the impact of HEIF funding. They should also evaluate the feasibility of reforming the KEF so that it becomes a CKEF (Civic and Knowledge Exchange Framework), ensuring there is an evaluation on the economic and social impact on a university’s town, city and region that goes beyond KE activity so it is providing a holistic picture. Following the formal link between CKEF and HEIF the Government should look to increase the allocation of HEIF from £284m in 2026–27 to at least £500m annually.

7. Reweighting existing measurement criteria

As part of or following on from the wider Tertiary/HE Review (see below), the Treasury alongside Research England and the OfS should review the feasibility of redirecting and/or reweighting existing funding mechanisms – QR, REF, HEIF, and R&D tax credits. The emphasis would be on changing criteria, weightings, and conditions to incentivise place impact, including a cost/benefit analysis for any proposed change.

C. Civic at the centre of system change

Alongside the issue of ownership and interim incentives, it is vital that the civic/place agenda is front and centre of any wider change to the higher education system: place should be one of the terms of any future settlement, not an afterthought.

8. Place and the tertiary review

If and when the Government launches a major review (a new Dearing, for example) of the higher education or broader tertiary system, it must include ‘place’ as a key part of its terms of reference for that review, so that the system’s impact on place is a major feature of whatever settlement the review reaches. In other words, that review would need to consider the full impact of the reforms and system on local places, including skills and discipline provision, innovation and business as well as cultural engagement.

9. Single department for HE, skills and research

Building on the recommendation set out in The Post-18 Project’s report A Ministry for Manchesterism10 and the ambitions set out in the Government’s Rewiring the State statement, the Government should remove higher education from the Department for Education and create a single department for HE, Skills, Innovation, Science, Research and Business. This department would, among several priorities, be tasked to ensure the broad HE and Research system contributes to economic and social wellbeing in ‘every postcode’.

full_text:
Following the issues with Microsoft, you may have missed some our recent blogs. To read Friday’s blog authored by Daniel Gilbert discussing HERA click here, or to read our weekend reading blog about the Renters Rights Act from Martin Blakey, click here.

This blog was kindly authored by Dr Samantha Durrant, Lecturer at the University of Manchester.

Universities collect extensive data about widening participation students, but how often do we ask those students what the label means to them or whether they recognise the support attached to it as being for them?

Widening participation encompasses overlapping characteristics and circumstances, including deprivation, ethnicity, disability, age and care experience, making it difficult to identify how many students meet these criteria. Office for Students data show that 24.9 per cent of full-time undergraduate entrants in 2023/24 came from the most deprived areas of England, yet institutional evidence remains stronger on who students are and the outcomes they achieve than on how they understand the widening participation label and the associated support available.

Universities are increasingly expected to include the student voice as part of decision-making processes, but what is less often asked is how intended recipients understand the widening participation label itself, whether they recognise targeted provision as relevant to them, or why eligible students do not engage (Rahman, 2025). Academics and professional support staff may consequently design and communicate well-intentioned provision around assumptions rather than the needs of the students.

In 2026, I surveyed 24 widening participation students at one UK university about how they understood widening participation, whether they identified with the categorisation, and how this related to belonging, participation and support. The study was small and exploratory, so its findings are tentative. However, the responses illuminate a gap that the broader institutional metrics alone cannot capture: the distance between being eligible for support and recognising that it is relevant, acceptable and accessible.

The resulting paradox is that categories which reveal inequality at sector level can fail at the point of delivery. If students do not understand the terminology, identify with the label or feel able to disclose the circumstances behind it, provision that depends on self-recognition and self-referral misses many of its intended recipients.

What students said

Only 17 per cent of the students reported participating in or receiving targeted widening participation support, while a further 21 per cent were unsure whether they had received any. This does not establish that provision was absent but raises a more revealing question: can students identify widening participation support and recognise whether they are eligible for it?

I wasn’t made aware that this was something I could seek extra support for.

Students valued widening participation as language for naming inequality, yet some felt uncomfortable when it was applied to them, associating it with pity, charity or being marked as different. Others met an institutional criterion without seeing themselves as disadvantaged. Eligibility is an administrative judgement; identity is personal and contextual. Treating the two as interchangeable risks designing support around a label that some intended recipients neither recognise nor accept.

I don’t like that I’m placed in another category as other students, or that I’m labelled differently.

Students reported concerns about belonging and representation, particularly those who met multiple widening participation criteria. Some felt different from peers who appeared more financially secure or familiar with university culture. These accounts suggest that a formally available service may still feel socially distant from the students it is intended to support.

There is a wider conversation about not just participating in but thriving and belonging in higher education.

Students’ experiences also highlighted why support must be easy to recognise and use. Barriers included paid work, living costs, caring responsibilities and unfamiliar institutional processes. Without family experience of higher education, practical processes such as accommodation, registration, mitigating circumstances and graduation could feel daunting. The issue is not a lack of ability, but the expectation that students know how to independently find and interpret routes to information and support.

Finally, students challenged the idea that widening participation students are a homogeneous group. They may meet one criterion or several, identify with disadvantage or reject that framing, and need different forms of support. They also described many positive aspects of their experiences, including resilience, self-advocacy, peer support and contributions to change. A shared category can reveal patterned inequality, but it cannot produce a shared identity or a single set of needs.

What needs to happen next

The answer is not simply more initiatives or categories, but provision designed around the whole student lifecycle from eligibility to recognition, trust and use. The Office for Students’ Equality of Opportunity Risk Register identifies unequal access to information and guidance, insufficient academic support and insufficient personal support as risks across the student lifecycle. Universities need to ask not only whether an intervention exists, but who knows about it, who uses it, who does not and why.

Universities must involve students in designing, communicating and evaluating support. This should include students who did not engage, with a particular focus on understanding why. Communications should use clear, recognisable language and explain what support is available without requiring students to align with a particular identity. Wherever possible, services should reduce repeated self-disclosure, offer multiple routes into support and equip academic advisers to signpost sensitively without assumptions or stigma.

Categories remain essential for exposing inequality, but successful widening participation cannot be judged by eligibility or provision alone. Institutions need to know whether students recognise support, trust it and can use it without stigma or unnecessary disclosure. Students should not only be counted within a category; they should help determine whether the support attached to it works.

title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
summary:
Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked

The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”

This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “human bandwidth”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

full_text:
The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”

This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “human bandwidth”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

Trust in institutions is waning. Reliability and fair outcomes matter. But the public also need ways to challenge decisions. Learning from business must not mean treating public scrutiny as “frictions” or neglecting the people whom markets fail to serve. Dame Antonia correctly identifies poor incentives, churn and inadequate training as issues. But who gets to the top also matters. A 2025 paper by Oxford University’s Erzsébet Bukodi and John H Goldthorpe, with Nottingham University’s Inga Steinberg, says access to elite civil service posts remains skewed to people from advantaged backgrounds. Progress towards widening access has reversed in the last 20 years. Whitehall risks overlooking the talent to govern an increasingly complex country.

The academics traced the backgrounds of 476 public service leaders between 1945 and 2022. Among officials reaching the top, the share from higher professional and managerial families fell from 56% before 1960 to 45% in 1980-99, then rose again. Those reaching senior posts in 2000‑22 resembled their pre-1960 predecessors in class origins. The paper also highlights how few people at the top have qualifications in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) or quantitatively oriented disciplines such as sociology and demography. The latter could help officials understand the lives affected by policies they implement. Such a “cultural disconnect”, experts say, has caused major policy blunders.

title: How a class on climate change leaves students feeling ‘energized’
summary:
Jeffrey Seidman holds a doctorate in philosophy. He spent much of his first two decades as a college professor helping students interpret texts by writers like Aristotle, Plato and Kant. And yet Seidman, of Vassar College, also teaches one of the most compelling classes on climate change I’ve come across. The course, Climate Solutions and […]

The post How a class on climate change leaves students feeling ‘energized’ appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Jeffrey Seidman holds a doctorate in philosophy. He spent much of his first two decades as a college professor helping students interpret texts by writers like Aristotle, Plato and Kant. And yet Seidman, of Vassar College, also teaches one of the most compelling classes on climate change I’ve come across.

The course, Climate Solutions and Climate Careers: Finding Your Place in the Climate Fight, teaches students about the technologies, policies and strategies behind the clean energy transition, and how to advance them. It’s built on the idea that virtually every career — in fields as diverse as law, finance, education and urban planning — can play a role in combating the climate crisis.

Students spend two classes per week studying solutions, such as electrifying transportation, greening the grid and bringing clean energy to the developing world. On Fridays, they hear from an outside speaker whose career is devoted to advancing climate solutions. Past speakers have included Emma Fisher, co-founder of Climate Cabinet, which backs candidates for local and state office who are supportive of climate action, and Zoe Samuel, a venture partner at Starshot Capital, which invests in climate technology like ultra-efficient heat pumps and food additives to reduce livestock methane emissions. Seidman also runs a website to bring lessons from his class to a wider audience.

I recently spoke with Seidman about his course, which he has taught since 2021. At the end of our conversation, he issued a sort of call to arms to other liberal arts professors to step outside of their disciplines and help educate students about the seismic clean energy transition happening around them. Not doing so, he said, does a disservice to students — and the planet.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

You are a philosopher by training, and yet you’re teaching a class on climate solutions and careers. How did that happen?

I like teaching philosophy a lot — I think it’s valuable and makes people’s lives richer. But sometime around 2020ish, as the world was more and more visibly on fire, continuing to do what I was doing felt sort of morally indefensible for me. I began to think hard about leaving academia and trying to find a job where I could spend my working hours trying to move the ball forward on climate. At some point I realized I was 50ish, I had a mortgage and a kid in college, and by the time I retooled and retrained that probably wouldn’t be the most useful thing or the way I could be the most impactful.

I decided the best thing I could do would be try to leverage the role I already had. Right around this time, I read the collection of essays “All We Can Save.” The essayists, they are all women, are very diverse in what they do — some do policy, some are activists, some are in finance. But they are all finding ways to address the climate problem. I got the idea partly from this book for a course that would help students do what I wish I could do if I were 20 years old, which is to find a way to a career in climate.

How does the course help students do that?

The way I conceived of it was twofold. One was understanding the shape of the problem, sector by sector. So, transportation is roughly a third of emissions, and buildings are roughly a third of emissions, and agriculture and land use, depending on how you count it, is a third to a quarter of emissions. And then figuring out what are climate solutions in agriculture, etc.

It’s also helping students broaden their imaginations of what a climate career might be. A lot of students, if you say climate career, they might think climate scientist, activist/organizer, maybe they think politician. And the list stops there.

But we need all the skills. We’re talking about transforming the basis of the whole global economy. And it is going to touch everything, so we need just about every skill. We need storytellers to move narratives, we need architects and urban planners, we need people to negotiate community benefit agreements for renewable energy developers.

What kind of knowledge do your students come in with and where do they end up?

They are really pessimistic, they feel doomed and anxious and scared. Not that any of that is inappropriate — it’s not, and I absolutely don’t believe there’s a right thing to feel. But they do not have a sense of just how much progress there has been. If you look at a pie chart of emissions, three-quarters comes from energy in one way or another. Today we have a recipe for this: Green the grid, and electrify everything. We are going to win this. It’s a question of how much pain and suffering and death and species extinction there is along the way — I am not trying to be overly Pollyannaish. But the energy transition will happen.

Students come out, I think, much more energized. There’s a path to success, and we can do this. And the more people who contribute to this, the faster it goes. That’s motivating.

How has the class evolved since you started teaching it five years ago?

The basic content of the class hasn’t changed all that much; my learning goals for the class have gotten refined. I sort of homed in slowly on three. One is being able to explain things. One assignment has to do with explaining a climate solution — some technology, some policy idea, something else — to a normal audience who doesn’t know anything about it. The students get to choose the medium, anything from standup comedy, design card games, write songs, digital interactives, zines, a podcast.

A second learning goal is advocating for stuff. The climate movement has been great at churning out white papers and mounds of evidence. But the other side has been so effective for so long at using all the tools of public relations. If we don’t do that, we are playing with hands behind our back. I have an assignment where students have a choice of making social media videos or writing letters to the editor, where the goal isn’t simply to inform you, it’s to try to figure out communications strategies that actually reach people and make them click or read.

I also have students find — and I give them resources to help them find — random people whom they don’t know who have some sort of climate career. They can use the Work on Climate Slack room to help find people. On LinkedIn, there is #OpenDoor Climate. People who have that in their LinkedIn profile are happy to be talked to about climate, and have a climate career. I have them reach out to — cold call, cold email — someone who has some sort of climate career and interview them over Zoom and edit it into a nice compact interview.

There’s a push for the liberal arts to seem more directly relevant to what students are going to go on to do career-wise. Do you see your class fitting into that?

Yes and no. First of all, I hate that push. I think it’s really valuable, and also good for people’s careers, to spend time not oriented around deliverable skills. However, practically, that is sort of what this course is about. What it is doing — and this is kind of a liberal artsy thing to do — is it is kind of multidisciplinary.

This course doesn’t do any one thing, like learn about the energy system or climate policy or urban planning, as well as a course in one of those things would. But what it does do is give a syncretic overview of how these parts fit together into a whole.

Anything else you’d like to share?

As an academic, you are trained in some field, and stepping outside of your field is so far outside of our comfort zones. But the thing is, to be useful to our students and give them something genuinely valuable, we only have to know a little more than them. As much as we like to be the authoritative person in the room who has our doctoral research to fall back upon, most of our disciplines, especially in liberal arts colleges, are not set up to equip students with thinking about solutions.

I have lots and lots of students who have taken many courses with climate change in the title, and they are all so depressed and feel we are doomed. They have taken courses in sociology and literature and earth science, and no one has told them there’s this amazing revolution going on in the way we use energy. Especially for liberal arts colleges, I feel like if we don’t talk about solutions, we are doing an active disservice to our students.

We are on the cusp of transformations that will remake the whole world, socially, environmentally, politically. A fossil fuel-powered world is a world where wealth and therefore political power are concentrated. Bill McKibben has this nice line that it’s the greatest wealth redistribution in world history.

We need to be teaching this. And that means we need to be educating ourselves beyond the bounds of our discipline. If not, we are doing a gross disservice to our students, and they leave dispirited and they think, ‘I might as well go join a private equity firm or go work for Deloitte.’

Help them see there’s something really positive to join. They are hungry for that.
