full_text:
Hundreds of students at the University of Melbourne were forced to abandon their final exams on Monday morning after many were unable to access the digital platform needed to begin them.

Jol Scobie, a first-year student at the university, was set to take his Australian politics exam on Monday after preparing for weeks. He had initially been told earlier in the year it was going to be a hand-written essay before instructors changed the test to a digital platform.

The subject was one of several holding exams at the Royal Exhibition Building in Carlton, with hundreds of students in attendance on Monday. About half were able to log on to the digital system and begin, Scobie said, but many others were left sitting at their desks, staring at a blank screen for about 50 minutes.

Students undertaking the Australian politics exam were meant to complete two 1,000-word essays over two hours.

“The [exam coordinators] said: ‘Listen, we can’t get it to work. It’s time for everyone to leave,’” Scobie said. “We were sort of standing there watching hundreds and hundreds of students pour out of the building.”

A university spokesperson confirmed technical issues caused the cancellation of a “small number” of exams on both 11 and 16 November.

“Early indications are that the issue relates to third-party technical partners involved in the delivery of our digital exams,” the spokesperson said. “Our teams are following established contingency processes to resolve the issue and communicate alternative arrangements for the students affected.

“We understand exam disruptions can be stressful for our students, and have support services available to assist students as needed.”

The university did not immediately reply to questions about how many students were affected, and if they would be able to sit makeup examinations before Friday.

Millie Mountford, another first-year student, said there had been limited communication about when a makeup exam would be held and when students and the university would be able to fit them in during an already busy week. Thousands of other students will be sitting their own tests in the coming days, with Mountford herself having another scheduled for tomorrow.

She does not know if it will go forward without any issues.

“I’m just kind of demotivated to study when I don’t even know if it will actually be worth it,” she said. “It’s just majorly inconvenient.”

Charlotte Wickham said the cancelled exam could snarl her travel plans to see her family in Tasmania over the holiday break due to the high cost and limited ability to change flights at the last minute.

“The stress really comes from not knowing if they are going to reschedule [the exams for] the supplementary period,” she said. “We have these questions that we’ve specifically studied for and now we have such a long period of waiting. We’ve planned our lives, and we have to keep these at the back of our minds. Do we have to restudy because the questions are different?”

The issues come after the National Tertiary Education Union organised a 24-hour strike and four-day teaching ban in October amid concerns from members about academic workloads, AI protections and fair pay. Members voted to approve a proposed new enterprise agreement to address some of those concerns earlier in November.

title: Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement
summary:
The First Five Minutes: Traps and Snap Judgments You walk into classroom 531 on the fifth floor, on a missive to deliver your best first lecture of the fall semester. You smile and say hello to your new students, expecting a wave of friendly faces in return. A few look up from their laptops and […]

The post Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The First Five Minutes: Traps and Snap Judgments

You walk into classroom 531 on the fifth floor, on a missive to deliver your best first lecture of the fall semester. You smile and say hello to your new students, expecting a wave of friendly faces in return. A few look up from their laptops and grin back, and you instantly decide these will be the “easy” students who like you best. You like them best, too. You take your place at the podium when a student texting on their phone catches your eye. A sudden thought flits across your mind: this student may be trouble. Just like that, assumptions are formed before class even begins. First impressions can stick.

From an evolutionary standpoint, this urge to make snap judgments makes you more than just judgy. It is an adaptive survival mechanism rather than a superficial flaw (Zebrowitz, 2017). Our human ancestors had to rapidly assess the lay of the land to detect threats, so gut reactions kept them safe. But in a modern college classroom free from creatures and carnivores, that ancient instinct can lead to a severe misassessment of the terrain. When a student meets your greeting with silence or a blank stare, their quiet response most likely has nothing to do with you.

Deciphering the Blank Stare

A flat expression is not an automatic sign of hostility, an indictment of your teaching, or a sign of personal animosity. In reality, a reserved student is usually dealing with one of a dozen unspoken realities. The quiet one in the back might be a first-generation student who has never stepped foot inside a college classroom. Another might be experiencing imposter syndrome, afraid to stand out. Some students simply land lower on the extroversion or openness scales, while others may be dealing with physical or mental health challenges that make emotional expressions more difficult to muster. It could simply be that they are daydreaming, having a difficult day, or lost in a laptop screen.

While managing screens is a real challenge—one that can be addressed by keeping a room mostly tech-free and offering old-school notebooks and pens as incentives as I do—the main takeaway is simple. An inexpressive or stoic student is not an adversary. But it makes sense why your brain may register them as one. When someone gives you a still face, you instinctively flag the expression as a threat to the relationship. Because humans are meaning-makers, we interpret a blank face as rejection. Inattention and disengagement may be just as damaging as actual conflict because it leaves you stuck in an uncertain state, wondering if you matter to the other person (Tronick, 1989).

The Neural Overlap of Rejection

This connection between social rejection and physical pain is deeply biological. Research from a meta-analysis of over 500 published studies shows that when rejection is powerfully elicited, like having someone who recently experienced an unwanted breakup view a photograph of their ex-partner, the specific brain regions that support the sensory components of physical pain, such as the secondary somatosensory cortex and the dorsal posterior insula, become highly active (Kross et al., 2011).

This means that social heartbreak and physical injury share the same neural real estate. When brain scans look at someone experiencing severe rejection, the areas lighting up are the same ones that register an actual physical injury, like a broken bone or a burn. Your brain does not distinguish between a wounded body and a wounded ego. These results give literal meaning to the idea that rejection hurts! It is no surprise that our language equates social pain and estrangement with words typically reserved for physical injury, like being crushed, shattered, or having a broken heart (Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004).

From Cooing to Crying: The Psychology of the Blank Face

It is human nature to like people who like us. We tend to withdraw from those who shun us with a still face. This phenomenon traces back to Edward Tronick’s famous psychology experiment, which demonstrated how a mother’s neutral, still face left a baby feeling sequestered and scared.

To visualize this, picture a mother and her baby interacting, facing each other, smiling, and playing. Everything feels warm and connected. Suddenly, the mother goes completely blank. No smile, no reaction, just a neutral, stony expression, like her face just went on pause. At first, the baby tries to get her attention by smiling, cooing, and waving their little arms. When that fails, confusion turns to frustration. Some babies cry or scream before eventually collapsing into a state of helpless withdrawal. From their perspective, the safe emotional connection is gone, and they cannot get it back (Tronick et al., 1978).

The Trap of the Negative Narrative

Babies are hardwired to demand social reciprocity, but professors enjoy no such evolutionary leverage. While it’s hard not to react negatively to a face that seems unwelcoming,

We cannot throw a tantrum, scream, or shake our fists in the air to force a student to pay attention, smile back at us, or put their phone away. Likewise, publicly singling out a seemingly disengaged student with a sarcastic or critical remark is never effective. This can easily fracture the classroom climate and make everyone feel uncomfortable. A successful classroom fosters group cohesion, creating the emotional bond and sense of belonging that transforms a room of individuals into a supportive learning community (Yalom & Leszcz, 2020). Without that foundational safety, trust can evaporate and tension can spread.

I teach in the psychology department, so I’d like to think that my background has helped me foster a more patient, caring perspective toward students. When I walk into a classroom and cheerfully ask, “How was your break?” and am met with indifference by a few students, I am aware of the importance of avoiding snap judgements or viewing the class as an amorphous whole. Teachers who assume a class is distant or chilly will naturally start to pull back to protect their own warmth.

Attachment Styles in the Classroom

Instead of worrying about rejection, instructors can zoom out and recognize that “still faces” may reflect a student’s childhood attachment style. Avoidant and anxious individuals tend to maintain the same behavioral patterns in school as they do in their interpersonal relationships, using attachment as an innate emotion regulation system to modulate stress (Fraley & Roisman, 2019).

When we view the classroom through this lens, we can cautiously seek out the students who may never otherwise visit our office hours. According to research by Gore and Rogers (2010), a student’s childhood attachment style significantly influences how they handle academic goals. Their study found that securely attached students tend to thrive and earn higher grades when their academic motivations are tied to the interests of important people in their lives. In other words, when a secure student knows their parents are proud of them, or when they have a professor who checks in on them, it acts like fuel. They think, “People care about me and want me to succeed,” and that makes them study harder and get better grades.

In contrast, avoidant students may eschew the involvement of others. Even when a professor reaches out with genuine support, offers help, or tries to learn about their goals, an avoidant student may panic. To them, your involvement feels like pressure, control, or a trap (Gore & Rogers, 2010). From the theoretical perspective of Rentzios and Karagiannopoulou (2021), this behavior is an intentional, self-protective strategy used to regulate overwhelming emotions during the learning process. Because avoidant students may view closeness with an authority figure (the professor) as dangerous or unstable, they might keep that bonding instinct firmly turned off, projecting a lack of interest.

In this way, a student’s blank gaze, apparent boredom, or surface-level effort is actually a sophisticated psychological defense mechanism (Rentzios & Karagiannopoulou, 2021). It is a behavioral pattern meant to avoid emotional risk by keeping both the course material and the professor at a safe, non-threatening distance.

Making Space in Room 531

In my classroom, I’m not trying to force an introverted or anxious student to become a bubbly extrovert. I’m just trying to show them that I am a reliable, safe professional. When an avoidant student realizes that their still face doesn’t make me upset, lose energy, or pull back my support, their defense system often slowly begins to deactivate.

I believe the worst thing a teacher can do is give up on a quiet, reserved class by delivering a cold or distant lecture. Instead, we must show up with the same level of enthusiasm, structure, warmth, and clarity every single week. Ultimately, a blank face is not a personal insult or a threat to our authority. Once we drop defensiveness or snap judgments, we create space for genuine connection, setting the stage for a positive classroom culture that supports learning and growth.

Beverly Wertheimer, PsyD, DMin, LCSW, teaches in the graduate school of psychology at Pepperdine University and is winner of the 2026 national Adjunct Faculty Excellence in Teaching Award from the Society for the Teaching of Psychology, a division of the American Psychological Association. Dr. Wertheimer is a child and adolescent psychotherapist, certified life coach, and author specializing in pedagogy and mental health. She has a background in broadcast journalism, including correspondent stints at ABC and NBC affiliates, as well as CNN’s entertainment news programs.

References

Eisenberger, N. I., & Lieberman, M. D. (2004). Why rejection hurts: A common neural alarm system for physical and social pain. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 8(4), 189–200. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2004.05.010

Fraley, R. C., & Roisman, G. I. (2019). The development of adult attachment: A long-term longitudinal study of NICHD study of early childcare and youth development. Psychological Science, 30(6), 825–838.

Gore, J. S., & Rogers, M. J. (2010). Why Do I Study? The Moderating Effect of Attachment Style on Academic Motivation. The Journal of Social Psychology, 150, 560-578.

E. Kross, M.G. Berman, W. Mischel, E.E. Smith, & T.D. Wager. (2011). Social rejection shares somatosensory representations with physical pain. National Academy of Sciences. 108 (15) 6270-6275, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1102693108

Rentzios, C. and Karagiannopoulou, E. (2021) Rethinking Associations between Distal Factors and Learning: Attachment, Approaches to Learning and the Mediating Role of Academic Emotions. Psychology, 12, 899-924. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2021.126055

Tronick, E. Z. (1989). Emotions and emotional communication in infants. American Psychologist, 44(2), 112–119. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.44.2.112

Tronick, E., Als, H., Adamson, L., Wise, S., & Brazelton, T. B. (1978). The infant’s response to entrapment between contradictory messages in face-to-face interaction. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 17(1), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0002-7138(09)62273-1

Yalom, I. D., & Leszcz, M. (2020). The theory and practice of group psychotherapy (6th ed.). Basic Books.

title: From COP31 to Antarctica: Two UK alumni tackling climate change
summary:
Climate action takes many forms. For two Australia-based graduates of UK institutions, it means caring for the young people taking part in global negotiations, and looking back across millennia to understand how the natural world has changed.

Georgia Monaghan, co-founder of ECOMIND, and Dr Theresa Cole, a researcher at Adelaide University, are the Australian recipients of the British Council's Alumni UK Grant Programme 2026–27. Each grant is worth up to £5,000 ($9,600 AUD) and is designed to help alumni turn climate action ideas into reality.

Alumni UK is the British Council's global network for international graduates of a UK education, including those who studied transnationally or online. Launched in 2022, it offers events, webinars, grants, scholarships and competitions, and helps alumni connect and collaborate. The 2026–27 grants support alumni-led projects on climate change, sustainability, inclusion and inequality. In Australia, this round focused on climate action and sustainability.
full_text:
An Australian charity co-founder and an Adelaide researcher have each received a British Council Alumni UK Grant. One is supporting young delegates at the UN climate talks. The other is reading around 50,000 years of history in Antarctic seabird deposits.

Climate action takes many forms. For two Australia-based graduates of UK institutions, it means caring for the young people taking part in global negotiations, and looking back across millennia to understand how the natural world has changed.

Georgia Monaghan (pictured above right), co-founder of ECOMIND, and Dr Theresa Cole (pictured above left), a researcher at Adelaide University, are the Australian recipients of the British Council's Alumni UK Grant Programme 2026–27. Each grant is worth up to £5,000 ($9,600 AUD) and is designed to help alumni turn climate action ideas into reality.

Alumni UK is the British Council’s global network for international graduates of a UK education, including those who studied transnationally or online. Launched in 2022, it offers events, webinars, grants, scholarships and competitions, and helps alumni connect and collaborate. The 2026–27 grants support alumni-led projects on climate change, sustainability, inclusion and inequality. In Australia, this round focused on climate action and sustainability.

The grants are part of British Council Australia’s year-long programme of climate and environmental work marking COP31, the UN Climate Change Conference. COP31 runs in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November, with Australia holding the role of President of Negotiations.

Helen Salmon, Director, Australia at the British Council, said the grants support those already working to achieve change.

“When we opened these grants, we wanted to back people already leading climate action in their communities,” she said.

“Georgia and Theresa show how far that reaches, from supporting young advocates at COP31 to tracing around 50,000 years of change in Antarctica. Climate and environment are woven through our strategy at the British Council in Australia. These initiatives demonstrate the breadth of the response that is urgently required.”

Wellbeing at COP31

UN climate talks can be draining, especially for young people. ECOMIND, Australia’s leading youth climate mental health and wellbeing charity, is running a dedicated Wellbeing Corner in the Children and Youth Pavilion at COP31.

Georgia Monaghan, its co-founder, spent a semester at the University of Leeds in 2014 while completing her degree at the University of Newcastle.

The Corner offers peer support, mental health first aid and counselling triage. A buddy system pairs first-time delegates with experienced ones, and daily workshops focus on creativity, connection and mindfulness. Before the conference, peer supporters and delegates completed the ECOMIND Certificate training, with debrief sessions to follow afterwards.

For Ms Monaghan, the grant is about more than practical support.

“Receiving this grant is recognition that how we do climate work matters as much as what we achieve,” she said.

“Young delegates arrive at COP carrying enormous hope and pressure, and too often they leave burnt out. Looking after the people doing the work is how we make sure the outcomes last.”

The funding covers the essentials that make the Corner possible: refreshments to keep delegates nourished through long days, creative and wellbeing materials for reflection and rest, and resources for the peer supporters who care for young people when it matters most.

The project aims to reduce burnout among young climate leaders and help them sustain their advocacy for the long term. It also sets out to show why wellbeing support should become a standard feature of future COPs.

A history written in seabird deposits

Dr Theresa Cole graduated from the University of Stirling in 2011 and is now a Ramsay Fellow at Adelaide University. Her research starts with an unusual archive. Snow petrels are Antarctic seabirds that return to the same colonies for generations. Their stomach oil deposits, known as mumiyo, build up in layers over time, creating a natural record of the past.

A pilot study showed for the first time that mumiyo can preserve ancient DNA.

“Receiving this grant means I can move beyond the pilot study and undertake a full study of snow petrel populations in the Weddell Sea region,” Dr Cole said.

“We now know that DNA can be recovered from this material, something previously thought to be unachievable, and this project will allow us to explore these deposits like pages in a book, revealing a record of what snow petrels have encountered over time.”

The project will analyse 68 dated samples from Dronning Maud Land, in Antarctica’s Weddell Sea region, some up to around 50,000 years old. It aims to show how coastal ecosystems and food webs have shifted over millennia, helping scientists distinguish natural variation from human-driven change.

The samples are held at Durham University in the UK, and the work also brings together Adelaide University, the Australian Antarctic Division, the University of Cologne in Germany, and BGI Group in China. Its findings are intended to inform conservation, including the proposed Weddell Sea Marine Protected Area.

The two projects could hardly be more different. One supports young delegates in real time at COP31. The other draws on evidence laid down over tens of thousands of years. Together, they show how UK alumni in Australia are tackling climate change in their own ways.

Part of a wider programme

The Alumni UK Grants sit within a broader programme of British Council climate work across Australia. It includes exhibitions, artist residencies, grants, and long-term collaborations with organisations such as Creative Australia and Julie's Bicycle.

At COP31, Dr Jen Rae is joining British Council activities. She co-founded Creative Climate, the national peak body for arts and climate and a major multi-year British Council partner. Delegates can also tune in to Radio Climate, a First Nations and artist-led transmission project, and explore BILYA, a relational mapping platform grounded in First Nations protocols.

In Sydney, the British Council is Industry Partner for Es Devlin’s Come Home Again and a series of talks at the opening of Powerhouse Parramatta.

British Council Australia’s work on climate and with UK alumni will continue beyond COP31. To find out more about Alumni UK or join the network, visit britishcouncil.org/study-work-abroad/alumni-uk.
